title: Agree to Disagree More Often
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post makes the case that leaders should propose agreeing to disagree earlier and more often than they typically do. Its starting premise is that conflict escalates because disagreement feels like rejection or an attempt at control, so removing the demand to surrender a position lowers defensiveness. The author explains that the phrase changes the goal of the conflict from winning to understanding, which creates psychological space and often softens positions over time. A longer-term benefit is signaling that the relationship matters more than being right. The piece also sets a limit: the approach suits disputes over values, preferences or interpretations, not situations where someone's behavior must change. It closes by calling the move a skill rather than a surrender.
points: Agreeing to disagree reframes a dispute so each side seeks understanding instead of persuasion, which reduces defensiveness.
Leaders should offer it early, as soon as the other party seems entrenched or defensive, rather than as a last resort.
Accepting another person's right to a view paradoxically makes both sides more open to changing their minds later.
The practice teaches that the relationship does not depend on intellectual agreement, a building block of healthy workplaces.
It has a boundary: it fits values, tastes and interpretations, but not behavior that needs to change.
quotes: Conflict often escalates because disagreement feels like rejection, disrespect, or an attempt to control others. Once both parties know they don’t have to surrender their position, defensiveness usually fades.

Agreeing to disagree works to de-escalate a dispute because it changes the goal of the conflict. Instead of having to change the mind of the other party, each side focuses on understanding the other without needing to reach the same conclusion.

Accepting that the other party is entitled to their own point of view creates psychological space that is less combative and more comforting. Ironically, it often softens the position each party holds and makes them more open to accepting a different perspective on the issue in the future.
Agreeing to disagree also has a long-term implication. It teaches people to elevate the relationship above any issue in dispute and suggests the relationship matters more than being right.

Conflicts over values, preferences, politics, interpretations, subjective evaluations, and aesthetic tastes are prime examples. But leaders can’t use this approach when someone’s underlying behavior needs to change.
In that sense, agreeing to disagree is more skill than surrender. A relationship that can hold two different truths is stronger than one that demands a single truth.
